w: At 2,744m the Hochwanner is Germany's second-highest peak after the Zugspitze - though the lower Watzmann is often wrongly credited with that title. Its north face drops some 1,500m, among the tallest walls in the Northern Limestone Alps, yet the mountain stays obscure, hidden behind the Alpspitze and Hollentalspitze.
s: Germany's real second-highest peak, hidden from view
_facts: 2,744m, second-highest peak in Germany after the Zugspitze
North face drops c. 1,500m, among the highest in the Northern Limestone Alps
Watzmann often wrongly cited as second-highest instead

w: Kloster Ettal is a Benedictine monastery in the village of Ettal, between Oberammergau and Garmisch-Partenkirchen. As of 2005 its community numbered more than 50 monks, with another five at its daughter house in Wechselburg, making it one of the largest Benedictine houses anywhere and a major visitor attraction.
s: One of the largest Benedictine houses, deep in Bavaria
_facts: Benedictine monastery in Ettal, near Oberammergau and Garmisch-Partenkirchen
Community of 50+ monks as of 2005, plus 5 at Wechselburg
One of the largest Benedictine houses; major visitor attraction

w: The Grosse Olympiaschanze is a K-125 ski jump on the Gudiberg above Partenkirchen, the traditional stage for the Four Hills Tournament's New Year's Day jumping - one of ski jumping's biggest annual fixtures. It anchors a complex of smaller hills, the K-80, K-43 and K-20, built for training and junior competition.
s: Bavaria's New Year's Day ski jump on the Gudiberg
_facts: K-125 large hill on the Gudiberg, south of Partenkirchen
Traditional venue for Four Hills Tournament New Year's jumping
Part of a complex with K-80, K-43 and K-20 hills

w: Eibsee - yew lake - lies at 973m elevation directly beneath the Zugspitze, Germany's highest mountain, just 3.5km from its summit. The lake covers 177 hectares within the municipality of Grainau, sits 9km southwest of Garmisch-Partenkirchen, and, unusually for a lake this scenic, remains in private ownership.
s: A private lake at the foot of the Zugspitze
_facts: 973m elevation, 177.4 hectares, 9km SW of Garmisch-Partenkirchen
At the northerly base of the Zugspitze, 3.5km from the summit
Lies in Grainau municipality; privately owned

w: Built 1914-1916 by philosopher-theologian Johannes Muller with architect Carl Sattler, Schloss Elmau is a four-story castle with hipped roof and tower, set in a nature reserve at the foot of the Wetterstein between Garmisch-Partenkirchen and Mittenwald. Now a national monument, it doubles as concert hall and hotel.
s: A 1916 philosopher's castle, now concert hall and hotel
_facts: Built 1914-1916 by Johannes Muller and architect Carl Sattler
Four-story castle, national monument, in a Krun nature reserve
At the foot of the Wetterstein between Garmisch-Partenkirchen and Mittenwald
Now a concert hall and hotel

w: Long thought unclimbable after repeated failed attempts, the Schusselkarspitze fell in 1894 to Heinrich Moser and Oscar Schuster, who forced its north flank. The south face's great slabs, the Plattenfluchten, rank among the toughest climbs in the Northern Limestone Alps; a bothy sits near the summit.
s: Once unclimbable, tamed by two climbers in 1894
_facts: Peak in the eastern Wetterstein, Northern Limestone Alps
First climbed 1894 by Heinrich Moser and Oscar Schuster via north flank
South face slabs (Plattenfluchten) among the hardest local climbing
Permanent emergency bothy near the summit

w: This lake in southwest Garmisch-Partenkirchen was pressed into Olympic service in 1936, hosting the speed skating and ten of the Games' 37 ice hockey matches on its frozen surface, while the bobsleigh runs operated on the slopes right alongside it.
s: A frozen lake that hosted the 1936 Winter Olympics
_facts: Lake in southwest Garmisch-Partenkirchen
Hosted 1936 Winter Olympics speed skating and 10 of 37 ice hockey games
Bobsleigh events took place adjacent to the lake

w: The Plattspitzen straddle the German-Austrian border as the southern counterpart to the Zugspitze, linked by a ledge called the Plattumrahmung. It has three summits around 2,680m - Gatterlspitz, Mittelgipfel, Westgipfel - and in 1871 Hermann von Barth climbed all three solo, when the peak was called the Wetterschrofen.
s: The Zugspitze's southern twin, once called Wetterschrofen
_facts: 2,680m, Wetterstein, on German-Austrian border
Three summits: Gatterlspitz, Mittelgipfel, Westgipfel
First climbed 1871 by Hermann von Barth solo, from the Zugspitzplatt
Formerly known as the Wetterschrofen

w: The Hochblassen rises to 2,706m in the Wetterstein, with a subsidiary summit called the Signalgipfel just 8m lower. Hermann von Barth, the solo climber who was picking off first ascents across this range in 1871, took this one with a partner, Peter Klaisl, rather than alone.
s: A 2,706m Wetterstein peak first climbed in 1871
_facts: 2,706m, Wetterstein, Bavaria
Sub-peak Signalgipfel at 2,698m
First climbed 1871 by Hermann von Barth and Peter Klaisl
